analysis.title: Escalation after mid-terms? The calm before the storm (Mark Dowding, 30 October 2026)
key_insights: The Fed held rates at 3.88%. Treasury yields were little changed. Warsh did little to dispel expectations of hikes in December and Q1 next year, which would be three cumulative hikes unwinding the 2025 easing under Powell.
US inflation has exceeded target for close to six years. The report says the Fed is unlikely to take a more relaxed stance until inflation is on a declining path much closer to 2%.

US-Iran peace negotiations have largely stalled with neither side compromising. The report argues the pre-mid-term constraint on Trump avoiding an energy price spike will lift after the elections, raising escalation risk.

The report sees a strong US aversion to ground troops, and believes the IRGC expects any bombing campaign to deliver limited results. It puts the risk of a material escalation in the coming month at about 30%.

Escalation on both sides would push energy prices higher and add to the global inflation shock. On this basis the author thinks it is an opportune moment to close long duration positions in developed rates markets.
TTF gas futures topped €100 in the past week. Higher oil prices are sustaining Asian gas demand and Europe still needs to build stocks, so further upside is seen over the coming month.

Eurozone CPI is 3.8% and the report expects it to test 4.5%. It says the ECB will very likely need to hike in December and again in Q1. Lagarde announced her resignation as ECB Chair, starting a race for a successor, and the latest ECB meeting was relatively dovish in tone.

French stress has eased. Moody's retained France's Aa3 rating last Friday after OATs had been oversold at spreads wide of Albania. Having added French risk at the wides, the author is now inclined to reduce, as structural issues remain unresolved.

The UK Budget was largely a non-event. The Bank of England is expected to hike next week, with a dovish bias relative to other central banks, as the first of several hikes. Ofgem energy bills are seen rising 38.6% by next April, and the report says UK CPI is hard to see staying below 5%.
The report suggests a possible UK election in Q1 next year. Labour has been building a poll lead, and the author thinks Burnham may call it before the inflation and rate shock take hold.

The Bank of Japan held rates and kept its hiking bias. Markets project a hike to 1.5% in December, and the report expects 1.75% in June. After that, two political appointees by PM Takaichi should make the Board more dovish.

Japanese inflation is likely to rise less than elsewhere because falling rice prices weigh heavily in CPI. Rising domestic demand for JGBs, including retail participation, may support yields. Japanese markets remain very sensitive to overseas developments, which reduces conviction in a long duration stance.

Lula's surprise election victory over market-preferred Flavio Bolsonaro triggered a sharp Brazilian repricing. The currency fell 10% before bouncing and local rates rose over 250bps, with stop-loss pain a factor.

The report thinks Brazilian assets are overshooting, since Lula represents continuity and prices in the summer already assumed his win. A fiscal conservative such as Alckmin as Finance Minister could support a further retracement rally.
The dollar has continued to edge stronger, while FX volatility remains low relative to other asset classes.

AI-related credit spreads narrowed on hopes that recent hedge fund deleveraging was a market-clearing event. Sentiment in AI credit may stay fragile because AI debt and equity issuance continues, so investors need to sell assets to absorb supply. European credit lagged the US rally. Repricing means IG credit offers more value than in recent months.

The report expects Democrats to take clear control of both chambers of Congress in the mid-terms. It expects a push to impeach Trump, with the Democrats well short of the numbers needed, and some Republicans possibly distancing themselves from him.

Despite more value in yields and spreads than earlier this year, the author says it would be inappropriate to be too bearish now. The author stresses knowing when to add or reduce risk, and aims to add to positions during dislocations.

The author thinks it is an opportune moment to close long duration positions as energy-driven inflation and possible Middle East escalation add upside pressure to yields.

risk_factors: Material US-Iran escalation in the coming month, which the report puts at about 30% risk.
Energy-driven inflation from oil and gas pushing central banks to hike.
Policy error from a US administration with few willing to question the President.
Tighter monetary policy across the Fed, ECB, BoE and BoJ.
Persistent AI-related debt and equity issuance straining the market technical.
Housing market pain in the UK.
Japanese markets' sensitivity to overseas developments.
US political turmoil after the mid-terms, including impeachment pressure.
vol_and_positioning: FX volatility remains strikingly low relative to moves in other asset classes.
Stop-loss pain contributed to the Brazilian repricing, as investors were caught the wrong way.
Recent hedge fund deleveraging in AI credit may have been a market-clearing event.
geopolitical: US-Iran peace negotiations have largely stalled with entrenched positions on both sides.
Mid-term elections are seen as removing a perceived constraint on Trump taking escalatory action against Iran.
Hawks in the administration cite Iranian intent to accelerate its nuclear programme and want action sooner.
The US has a strong aversion to ground troops, and the IRGC expects a bombing campaign to deliver limited results.
Iran retains the ability to damage regional neighbours as a deterrent.
Lula won the Brazilian presidential election over Flavio Bolsonaro.
Moody's retained France's Aa3 rating and French stress eased.
A possible UK election in Q1 next year.
Takaichi is set to announce two political appointees to the BoJ Board.
Lagarde announced her resignation as ECB Chair.

tension_points.bull_case: Yields and spreads offer much more value than earlier this year, so the report cautions against being too bearish. Japan's falling rice prices and rising domestic JGB demand may also support bond markets.
tension_points.bear_case: Energy-driven inflation, possible US-Iran escalation and hikes from the Fed, ECB, BoE and BoJ argue for closing long duration positions.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A material US-Iran escalation within the coming month, put at about 30% risk, would push energy prices higher and strengthen the bear case.

tension_points.bull_case: Lula represents continuity, prices overshot relative to the summer, and a fiscal conservative such as Alckmin as Finance Minister could trigger a retracement rally.
tension_points.bear_case: Investors were caught the wrong way and stop-loss selling is driving the move, which the report calls a brutal repricing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Lula naming a Finance Minister who is not a fiscal conservative would undercut the retracement view.
